\begin{center}
\textbf{Abstract}
\end{center}

Research question: 'How did wage growth across Norwegian industries develop during the oil-price collapses of 2014 and 2020?'. The implementation of coding techniques is consistent with the literature and the lecture summaries. The main conclusion from this analysis is that both downturns introduced wage growth reduction. Despite this, the developments following were unequal.

# Introduction and objective

The oil industry represents a large share of the value creation in the Norwegian economy. For example, it makes up 18% of the Norwegian economy, 26% of the share of state revenues, 20% of total investmens and 42% of total exports (Ministry of Energy & Norwegian Offshore Directorate, 2026). Therefore understanding how oil price changes affect petroleum-related industries, employment and economic activity through wages is key. When considering these oil price shocks, it is natural to consider the advents of 2014 and 2020. Despite both downturns being measured in oil price, not all oil price shocks are not created equal. As we will see, the surrounding economic and financial conditions during these time periods differed, and these should be represented through the acquired data. 

This term paper wishes to understand the proposed mechanism of an oil price shock (2014 & 2020), and how these affected the wage growth. Here, we try to look at the wage growth preceding, during and following said shocks. This is in addition to looking at the intra-industries discrepancies. We also examined regional wages given the 2020 oil price shock as a form of comparison. 

From a coding perspective, this analysis attempts to combine the historical Brent Crude Oil Price futures with quarterly wage data from Statistics Norway (SSB). In this pursuit, a total of five SSB data sets are scraped and acquired to examine industry-level earnings, manufacturing wages, wage developments, and rationality. This analysis furthermore relied heavily on the workflow introduced from the lectures in that we start with acquiring the data, cleaning it, transforming it, and attempting to visualize it using R. To compare with the aforementioned time tables, year over year wage growth is calculated and comparisons are performed. 

The holistic purpose is not isolated to that of identifying causality like in an econometrics paper, it is to try and understand and juxtapose observed wage developments, on the one hand, with two historical economics shocks, on the other. This empiricism of how wage growth developed is affored because of this comparison.

## SSB API interaction:

# SSB 09175. We start with this one because it has the most coverage. 

SSB_09175 <- api_data_2(
  9175, # name of the table we are seeking to acquire.
  default_query = TRUE # specifying that all cells of metadata are included.
) # api_data_2() interacts with SSB API such that all
  # category nodes are preserved.

k09175 <- read_excel("09175.xlsx")

str(SSB_09175) # here we can see that this data-set is long. with 154 224 
               # rows across 5 columns

str(k09175) # here we can see that this data-set is very wide. There are 85 rows 
            # but with 3025 columns. 

# the purpose of downloading the xlsx file was to demonstrate and sanity check
# if the api interaction was correct. When comparing the str() of both, API
# data-set seems satisfactory. 

# For loop construction. The reasoning is simple: iteration. We have tested
# that the code above worked for the individual case. Now instead of copy 
# pasting five times, we can create a more sophisticated acquisition process. 

rm(k09175,SSB_09175) # start with clean slate. 

tables <- c(9175, 07219, 07235, 12314, 11654) # the name of each table.

SSB_metadata <- list() # empty list to store the metadata acquired. 

for (i in seq_along(tables)) {
  SSB_metadata[[i]] <- api_data_2(
    tables[i],
    default_query = TRUE
  )
} # we tell R that for every id in 'tables', we execute the api_data_2 function 
  # such that it acquires the relevant table metadata by communicating with 
  # SSB API. It then places these values in the list function we created
  # then after having done that for all the sets, we then rename these columns
  # to their original names already defined in order in 'tables'. 

names(SSB_metadata) <- tables # the order of the data frames is consistent
                              # with the order of the SSB tables in 'tables'.
                              # therefore, we can refer to each data directly
                              # through the list.

SSB_metadata[1] # refers to SSB table 9175 in the SSB_metadata list as [1].

for (id in names(SSB_metadata)) {
  assign(paste0("SSB_", id), SSB_metadata[[id]])
} # we know have extract each of the tables in a meaningful and understandable 
  # way. 


SSB_datasets <- c("SSB_9175", "SSB_7235", "SSB_7219", "SSB_12314", "SSB_11654")
# we create a new vector with the "" names of all data sets
for (i in SSB_datasets) {
  write.csv(get(i), paste0(i, ".csv"), row.names = FALSE)
}
# we make a for loop that downloads all of these for future reference.

```{r CLEANING, include=FALSE}

## BRENT

BRENT_DAILY <- BRENT |>
  pivot_longer(Mon:Fri, names_to = "day", values_to = "oil_price") |>
  mutate(
    week = ymd(str_extract(`Week Of`, "^\\d{4} [A-Za-z]+-\\s*\\d+")),
    date = week + match(day, c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")) -1
  ) |>
  select(date, oil_price) |>
  drop_na() |>
  arrange(date) # we know that the scraped BRENt was very messy, and too wide. 
                # we know remove the first column, and assign it date values
                # relative to the already established columns for the names
                # of each day of the weak. This is then pivoted, such that it is
                # descending relative from oldest to newest derived from the
                # dates and their numbers within each week. The second column
                # follows this pivot, but represents each oil price value assigned

head(BRENT_DAILY)

head(BRENT1)

tail(BRENT_DAILY)

tail(BRENT1)

sum(is.na(BRENT1))

BRENT1 <- na.omit(BRENT1)

# when comparing the first rows of both data frames. The conclusion is that
# scaping worked. With that said, this paper will opt to use the quantmod 
# FRED output given the extra sensitivity of the variables (one extra decimal)
# all NA's were removed. Therefore BRENT is the current object we will use.

BRENT <- BRENT1 

sum(is.na(BRENT))

BRENT1 <- na.omit(BRENT)

rm(BRENT_DAILY, BRENT1)

str(BRENT)

head(BRENT)

tail(BRENT)

ggplot(BRENT, aes(x = date, y = price)) + geom_line(color = "red") +

## SSB cleaning (in order)

str(SSB_11654)

str(SSB_12314)

str(SSB_7219)

str(SSB_7235)

str(SSB_9175)

# We can see that all data sets operate on a quarterly non-standardized frequency
# to make things more ready for time anchored operations, we should try to 
# standardize. This process is mentioned in lecture 3, when transforming; in
# lecture 6 when it comes to how R handles dates; and in lecture 7 when working 
# with structured data. Because we have five different data sets, we can 
# use a for loop executable:

class(SSB_metadata)

for (i in names(SSB_metadata)) {
  SSB_metadata[[i]] <- SSB_metadata[[i]] |>
    mutate(
      quarter = as.yearqtr(
        gsub("K", " Q", Tid),
        format = "%Y Q%q"
      )
    )
} # we tell r that for every i in SSB_metadata for each data set within the 
  # column "Tid" we replace the XXXXKX with XXXX Qx format. 

SSB_metadata[1] # we can see that the standardization effort worked with the 
                # addition of another variable "quarter"

# now that we have standardized, i would like to see how many NA values there
# are for each data set. I also want to see what statistical significance these
# NA values have for each data set. To simplify things, the best course is to
# again use a for loop. 

for (i in names(SSB_metadata)) {
  print(paste(
        i,
        round(mean(is.na(SSB_metadata[[i]]$value)) * 100, 2), 
        "%"))
}

# here we can see that the data set with the largest share of NA's is SSB_11654.
# Because we do not know which variable contains these NA's, we should do more
# investigative work 

for (i in names(SSB_metadata)) {
  print(
    SSB_metadata[[i]] |>
      group_by(ContentsCode) |>
      summarise(
        missing = sum(is.na(value)),
        percentage = mean(is.na(value)) * 100
      )
  )
}

# we can see that 9175 and 12314 have relatively low NA's counts, whereas
# 7219 & 7235 are totally complete. By virtue of 54% of 11654 is NA in terms of 
# the wage observations are missing, we should try to clean this one first. 
# We then need to understand if these NA's are of a statistical nature, or 
# if they are omitted for other reasons. The simple route would be to simply 
# NA omit everything, but before doing anything, it is important to see what is 
# the cause. This is in line with the lectures. 

SSB_metadata[["11654"]] |>
  filter(ContentsCode == "GjAvtaltMdlonn") |> 
  group_by(Region) |>
  summarise(
    missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    percentage = mean(is.na(value)) * 100
  ) |> 
  print(n = Inf)

# we can see that for counties (fylker) currently existing, and that had not 
# undergone a change in county structure, exhibit the fewest NA's. This is 
# important to consider because it could explain the variation in the NA's
# across counties. 


SSB_metadata[["11654"]] |>
  filter(ContentsCode == "GjAvtaltMdlonn",
         !is.na(value)
         ) |> 
  group_by(Region) |>
  summarise(
    first = min(quarter),
    last = max(quarter)
  ) |> 
  print(n = Inf)

# we can see that regions 03, 11, 15 & 18 have nearly full or full coverage 
# from the start to
# the end of the sample. These are Oslo, Rogaland, Møre og Romsdal and Nordland, 
# respectively. 

SSB_metadata[["11654"]] |>
  filter(ContentsCode == "GjAvtaltMdlonn",
         quarter >= 2018,
         quarter < 2023
  ) |> 
  group_by(Region) |>
  summarise(
    available = sum(!is.na(value)),
    missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    percentage = mean(!is.na(value)) * 100
  ) |> 
  print(n = Inf)

# the data shows that the countie politics of aggregation and seperation had
# massive disruptions in the availability of data. If we want to see NA's by 
# industry per the counties we are interest in, we can run another for loop

SSB_metadata[["11654"]] |>
  filter(Region %in% c("03", "11", "15", "18", "50"),
         ContentsCode == "GjAvtaltMdlonn",
         quarter >= 2018,
         quarter < 2023
  ) |> 
  group_by(Region, NACE2007) |>
  summarise(
    available = sum(!is.na(value)),
    missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 
  print(n = Inf)

# among the aforementioned counties we are interest in, all have continuous 
# wage observations needed for all the major industries were are concerned with 
# this is in relation to the set boundary of 2018 Q1, on the left tail, and
# 2023 Q4, on the right. 

RW_SSB_11654 <- SSB_metadata[["11654"]] |>
  filter(
    Region %in% c("03", "11", "15", "18", "50"),
    ContentsCode == "GjAvtaltMdlonn",
    NACE2007 != "00",
    NACE2007 != "00-99",
    quarter >= 2018, 
    quarter < 2023
  ) |> 
  select(Region, NACE2007, quarter, value) # we have now cleaned the 11654 
                                           # and reorganized the data such that
                                           # the aforementioned regions, adding
                                           # Trondheim, have been selected for 
                                           # all major industries. This means 
                                           # we can now compare how wages were  
                                           # before, during and after the 2020
                                           # oil price shock

str(RW_SSB_11654)
dim(RW_SSB_11654)
sum(is.na(RW_SSB_11654$value)) # no NA's now

# we can no proceed with SSB_12314

str(SSB_metadata[4])

# let us try to find NA's


SSB_metadata[["12314"]] |>

IW_SSB_12314 <- SSB_metadata[["12314"]] |>

MW_SSB_7235 <- SSB_metadata[["7235"]] |>
```

```{r TRANSFORMATION, include=FALSE}

## Brent 

# All of the SSB cleaned data sets are operating on a quarterly frequency. 
# this means that we need to scale up BRENT's frequency to match the limiting
# factor. 

BRENT_Q <- BRENT |> 
  mutate(quarter = as.yearqtr(date)) |>
  group_by(quarter) |>
  summarise(
    brent = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

str(BRENT_Q)

sum(is.na(BRENT_Q$brent))

ggplot(BRENT_Q, aes(x = quarter, y = brent)) + geom_line(color = "red") + 
  labs(
    title = "Quarterly BRENT",
    x = "Quarters",
    y = "USD per barrel"
  ) + theme_minimal() # looks very similar to the already used GGPLOT with daily
                      # oil prices. 

## SSB 12314

# with quarterly brent now accounted for with no NA values, we can proceed to 
# understand how to interact this with what we have in the existing SSB
# data sets. If we look at IW_SSB_12314, we can construct a new column that 
# accounts for the yearly changes in wage growth, measured in the the wages
# of the same industry in the same quarter in the year before. 

IW_SSB_12314 <- IW_SSB_12314 |> 
  group_by(NACE2007) |> 
  arrange(quarter, .by_group = TRUE) |> 
  mutate(
    wage_growth = (value / lag(value, 4) - 1) * 100 # this is the formula
  ) |> 
  ungroup()

str(IW_SSB_12314)

summary(IW_SSB_12314$wage_growth)

sum(is.na(IW_SSB_12314$wage_growth)) # 324 NA values for all quarters in the 
                                     # first four quarters of the first year
                                     # this is expected given our formula. 
                                     # because we have 81 industries, this lines
                                     # up perfectly with there being 81 x 4 = 
                                     # 324

IW_SSB_12314 |> 
  count(NACE2007, quarter) |>
  filter(n != 1) # every industry has one observation per quarter


## SSB 11654

RW_SSB_11654 <- RW_SSB_11654 |> 
  group_by(Region, NACE2007) |>
  arrange(quarter, .by_group = TRUE) |> 
  mutate(
    wage_growth = (value / lag(value, 4) -1 ) * 100 # formula notation
  ) |>
  ungroup()

str(RW_SSB_11654)

summary(RW_SSB_11654)

sum(is.na(RW_SSB_11654$wage_growth)) # now we are looking at the regional level
                                     # and because we have 16 industries (we 
                                     # we removed two) across 5 different counties
                                     # through 20 quarters. 16 * 4 * 5 = 320


## SSB 7219

HW_SSB_7219 <- HW_SSB_7219 |> 
  group_by(NACE) |> 
  arrange(quarter, .by_group = TRUE) |> 
  mutate(
    wage_growth = (value / lag(value, 4) -1)* 100
  ) |> 
  ungroup() # wage index growth column being added

str(HW_SSB_7219)

summary(HW_SSB_7219)

sum(is.na(HW_SSB_7219$wage_growth)) # because we have 16 industries, there will
                                    # will be missing values for each one 
                                    # in the starting year; 16 * 4  = 64

## SSB 7235

MW_SSB_7235 <- MW_SSB_7235 |> 
  group_by(NACE2007) |> 
  arrange(quarter, .by_group = TRUE) |> 
  mutate(
    wage_growth = (value / lag(value, 4) -1) * 100 # formula
  ) |> 
  ungroup()

str(MW_SSB_7235)

summary(MW_SSB_7235)

sum(is.na(MW_SSB_7235$wage_growth)) # 17 industries x 4 missing NA = 68


## SSB 9175 

str(HW_SSB_9175) # because in SSB_9175 wage growth is already accounted for,
                 # we do not need to conduct the same transformations 
                 # as all the other data sets

## final transformations

# let us look at whether there exists any large values in either direction 

summary(IW_SSB_12314$wage_growth)

summary(RW_SSB_11654$wage_growth)

summary(HW_SSB_7219$wage_growth)

summary(MW_SSB_7235$wage_growth)

# nothing stands out as being extreme (sanity check)

# we can proceed with checking if there are any instances where there exists
# 2 x obersvations 

IW_SSB_12314 |>
  count(NACE2007, quarter) |>
  filter(n > 1)

RW_SSB_11654 |>
  count(Region, NACE2007, quarter) |>
  filter(n > 1)

HW_SSB_7219 |>
  count(NACE, quarter) |>
  filter(n > 1)

MW_SSB_7235 |>
  count(NACE2007, quarter) |>
  filter(n > 1)

# as we can see there are no 2 x observations, which means the data we have 
# thus far satisfies transformation techniques such that the results we produce
# are credible. We can also continue by comparing these wage growth values with
# the orginal list data set SSB_metadata

SSB_metadata_GROWTH <- SSB_metadata[["7219"]] |>
  filter(ContentsCode == "Endring") |> 
  select(NACE, quarter, value) |>
  rename(SSB_metadata_GROWTH = value)

summary(SSB_metadata_GROWTH)

# now we compare the calculated changes with what is published by SSB. This is
# given through the "indeks" column and that, which contains the growth figures 
# published by SSB, and what we have caluclated through the formula
# is similar to this. 

compare_7219 <- HW_SSB_7219 |>
  left_join(SSB_metadata_GROWTH, by = c("NACE", "quarter")) |>
  mutate(
    difference = wage_growth - SSB_metadata_GROWTH
  )

summary(compare_7219$difference)

max(abs(compare_7219$difference), na.rm = TRUE)

head(compare_7219)

# as we can see the formula we used wage_growth = (value / lag(value, 4) -1)* 100
# seems to be very consistent with SSB's own "Endring" variable 

SSB_metadata_GROWTH <- SSB_metadata[["7235"]] |>
  filter(ContentsCode == "Endring") |> 
  select(NACE2007, quarter, value) |>
  rename(SSB_metadata_GROWTH = value)

compare_7235 <- MW_SSB_7235 |>
  left_join(SSB_metadata_GROWTH, by = c("NACE2007", "quarter")) |>
  mutate(
    difference = wage_growth - SSB_metadata_GROWTH
  )

summary(compare_7235$difference)

max(abs(compare_7235$difference), na.rm = TRUE)

head(compare_7235)

# while low values, we can see that compare_7235 > compare_7219. We can see if 
# the ten largest differences are noteworthy. It could seem that the reports
# from SSB_metadata were rounded up, which could explain why the difference 
# was greater in the latter, than the former data set. 

compare_7235 |>
  filter(!is.na(difference)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(difference))) |>
  select(NACE2007, quarter, wage_growth,
         SSB_metadata_GROWTH, difference) |>
  head(10)

# the wage growth variables in 7235 and 7219 seem satisfactory in terms of their
# validity. 

# we can continue with the other two variables, but it is important to highlight
# that while we use the same formula in transforming, there is no public indicy
# wrt. these wage growth numbers on the same "level" as what we have calculated
# already. Despite this, and because we have checked for duplicates, and the 
# NA values, these two latter data sets 12314 and 11654 seem satisfactory. 

rm(SSB_metadata_GROWTH, SSB_11654, SSB_12314, SSB_7219, SSB_7235, SSB_9175, 
   compare_7219, compare_7235)

#### BRENT INTEGRATION ####

# we integrate the quarterly brent numbers into the existing cleaned and
# transformed data sets. The goal is a consistent obersvation of brent per quarter
# we are assuming no duplicates, but we can check by:

BRENT_Q |>
  count(quarter) |>
  filter(n > 1) # zero rows -> no duplicates

range(BRENT_Q$quarter) # both tails more than capable to adapt to each data set

# let us also add a percentage change column to quarterly brent prices

BRENT_Q <- BRENT_Q |>
  arrange(quarter) |>
  mutate(
    brent_growth = (brent / lag(brent) - 1) * 100
  )

str(BRENT_Q) # new column added

sum(is.na(BRENT_Q$brent_growth)) # to be expected given what has already been
                                 # established
# to simplify the integration process, we should create the same list object
# that we started off with in SSB_metadata, but now with the cleaned and 
# transformed data sets. 

data <- list(
  "12314" = IW_SSB_12314,
  "11654" = RW_SSB_11654,
  "7219" = HW_SSB_7219,
  "7235" = MW_SSB_7235,
  "9175" = HW_SSB_9175
)

str(data) # it worked

SSB_CLE_TRA <- list()

for(i in names(data)) {
  SSB_CLE_TRA[[i]] <- data[[i]] |>
    left_join(BRENT_Q, by = "quarter")
} # we integrate brent quarterly into the existing cleaned and transformed
  # data sets. 

head(SSB_CLE_TRA[["12314"]])

head(SSB_CLE_TRA[["11654"]])

head(SSB_CLE_TRA[["7219"]])

head(SSB_CLE_TRA[["7235"]])

head(SSB_CLE_TRA[["9175"]])

for (i in names(SSB_CLE_TRA)) {
  assign(
    paste0("SCTI_", i),
    SSB_CLE_TRA[[i]]
  )
} # SCTI = SSB + CLEANED + TRANSFORMED + INTEGRATED

SCTI_7219 <- SCTI_7219 |>
  filter(quarter >= 2012, quarter < 2018)

SCTI_7219 <- SCTI_7219 |>
  mutate(
    period = case_when(
      quarter < as.yearqtr("2014 Q3") ~ "Before",
      quarter < as.yearqtr("2016 Q1") ~ "During",
      TRUE ~ "After"
    )
  ) # classified the data given their temporal anchoring 
    # with these we can continue with undertanding the before, during and after the
    # oil price collapse. 


SCTI_7235 <- SCTI_7235 |>
  filter(quarter >= 2012, quarter < 2018)

SCTI_7235 <- SCTI_7235 |>
  mutate(
    period = case_when(
      quarter < as.yearqtr("2014 Q3") ~ "Before",
      quarter < as.yearqtr("2016 Q1") ~ "During",
      TRUE ~ "After"
    )
  ) # classified the data given their temporal anchoring 
# with these we can continue with undertanding the before, during and after the
# oil price collapse. 

SCTI_9175 <- SCTI_9175 |>
  filter(quarter >= 2012, quarter < 2023)

SCTI_9175 <- SCTI_9175 |> 
  mutate(
    episode = case_when(
      quarter < zoo::as.yearqtr("2018 Q1", format = "%Y Q%q") ~ "2014 collapse",
      TRUE ~ "2020 collapse"
    )
  )


SCTI_12314 <- SCTI_12314 |>
  filter(quarter >= 2018, quarter < 2023)

SCTI_12314 <- SCTI_12314 |> 
  mutate(
    period = case_when(
      quarter < zoo::as.yearqtr("2020 Q1", format = "%Y Q%q") ~ "Before",
      quarter < zoo::as.yearqtr("2021 Q1", format = "%Y Q%q") ~ "During",
      TRUE ~ "After"
    )
  )


SCTI_11654 <- SCTI_11654 |>
  filter(quarter >= 2018, quarter < 2023)

SCTI_11654 <- SCTI_11654 |> 
  mutate(
    period = case_when(
      quarter < zoo::as.yearqtr("2020 Q1", format = "%Y Q%q") ~ "Before",
      quarter < zoo::as.yearqtr("2021 Q1", format = "%Y Q%q") ~ "During",
      TRUE ~ "After"
    )
  )



write.csv(SCTI_7219, "C7219.csv", row.names = FALSE)

write.csv(SCTI_7235, "C7235.csv", row.names = FALSE)

write.csv(SCTI_9175, "C9175.csv", row.names = FALSE)

write.csv(SCTI_12314, "C12314.csv", row.names = FALSE)

write.csv(SCTI_11654, "C11654.csv", row.names = FALSE)





rm(data, HW_SSB_7219, HW_SSB_9175, MW_SSB_7235, RW_SSB_11654, IW_SSB_12314)
```

```{r ECONOMIC ANALYSIS, include=FALSE}
#INDUSTRY NAMES for SSB 9175 using jsonlite

# Retrieve official industry names in English
SSB_labels <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  "https://data.ssb.no/api/pxwebapi/v2/tables/09175/data?lang=en",
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

# Here a Vector i linking codes to industry names
industry_names <- unlist(
  SSB_labels$dimension$NACE$category$label
)

# Check that industry codes and names were retrieved
head(industry_names)

# Add industry names to our existing dataset
SCTI_9175 <- SCTI_9175 |>
  mutate(
    industry_name = coalesce(
      unname(industry_names[NACE]),
      NACE
    )
  )

# Check the result
SCTI_9175 |>
  distinct(NACE, industry_name) |>
  print(n = Inf)


#### SIMPLE REGRESSION for SSB 9175 ####

# First we calcute the annual Brent price growth for the regression
BRENT_9175 <- BRENT_Q |>
  arrange(quarter) |>
  mutate(
    brent_yoy = (brent / lag(brent, 4) - 1) * 100
  ) |>
  select(quarter, brent_yoy)

# Adding annual Brent growth to SSB 9175
REG_9175 <- SCTI_9175 |>
  left_join(BRENT_9175, by = "quarter")

# Selecting oil and gas extraction industry
REG_9175_06 <- REG_9175 |>
  filter(
    NACE == "pub2X06",
    is.finite(value),
    is.finite(brent_yoy)
  )

# Afterwards we use nrow to check available observations
nrow(REG_9175_06)

# Using the if, stop method to check if there are no usable observations
if (nrow(REG_9175_06) < 3) {
  stop("Not enough complete observations")
}

# Here is the simple regression model
model_9175 <- lm(
  value ~ brent_yoy,
  data = REG_9175_06
)

# Examining the results
summary(model_9175)

# Using ggplot to visualize the model for SSB_9175

ggplot(REG_9175_06,
       aes(x = brent_yoy, y = value)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    color = "red"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Brent Price Growth, Wages and Salary Growth",
    subtitle = unique(REG_9175_06$industry_name)[1],
    x = "Annual Brent Price Growth (%)",
    y = "Annual Wages and Salary Growth (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

  mutate(
    industry_name = coalesce(
      unname(industry_names[NACE]),
      NACE
    )
  )

# Heatmap creation to visualize for all industries
p_heatmap <- ggplot(SCTI_9175_sum_comp,
                    aes(x = episode, y = industry_name, fill = during_difference)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white" ) +
  geom_text( aes(label = round(during_difference, 1)), size = 3) +
  scale_y_discrete( labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 35)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "red",
    mid = "white",
    high = "blue",
    midpoint = 0
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Industry Wages and Salary Growth During Oil Price Shocks",
    subtitle = "Change in average growth: During minus Before",
    x = "Oil Price Shock",
    y = "Industry",
    fill = "Change (pp)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10)
  )

print(p_heatmap)

# Creating a png
ggsave(
  "heatmap.png",

  width = 16,
  height = 24,
  dpi = 300
)
```
